nameStory: The dog pelt lichen gets its name from its supposed resemblance to a dog's hide or fur when dried and curled. This earthy comparison made sense to early naturalists who saw the brownish, leathery lobes as similar to animal pelts. The scientific name 'canina' literally means 'of the dog' in Latin, cementing this canine connection.
description: Dog pelt lichen is a leafy, foliose lichen that forms large, sprawling patches on soil and moss. Its broad, flat lobes spread outward like leather petals, creating colonies that can stretch several inches across. The upper surface is typically gray-green to brownish, while the underside reveals a pale belly with distinctive dark veins and scattered rhizines (root-like structures). When wet, the colors become more vibrant and the texture softens noticeably.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feel like soft leather or suede when dry, becoming more pliable and slightly spongy when moistened by rain or dew

idTips.label: Underside Pattern
idTips.description: Flip it over to see a pale whitish belly marked with dark brown or black veins radiating from the center, plus scattered dark, hair-like rhizines

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms rosette-like patches with broad, rounded lobes that overlap like shingles, often curling upward at the edges when dry

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to brownish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant blue-green or olive when wet

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes reach 1-3 inches wide, with entire colonies spanning 4-8 inches across

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on soil, moss, or humus - never directly on tree bark or rock surfaces

habitat: Look for dog pelt lichen in moist, shaded areas throughout New England's forests, particularly on moss-covered soil, rotting logs, and forest humus. It thrives in deciduous and mixed woodlands where moisture lingers, often found along stream banks, in ravines, or on north-facing slopes. You'll also spot it in older, undisturbed areas where the forest floor stays consistently damp.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the blue-green colors intensify and the texture becomes noticeably softer and more flexible.
seasonality.summer: May appear drier and more brownish, but still identifiable by the characteristic veined underside pattern.
seasonality.fall: Often partially hidden under fallen leaves but still visible and identifiable, with colors remaining fairly consistent.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round under snow cover, appearing darker and more leathery but maintaining its diagnostic underside features.

funFact: Dog pelt lichen was historically used in folk medicine to treat rabies and other dog-related ailments - not because it actually worked, but because people believed the 'Doctrine of Signatures' meant that things resembling body parts or animals could cure related problems!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pelt lichens in the same genus, but dog pelt lichen's combination of soil-growing habit and distinctly veined pale underside sets it apart. Memory trick: 'Dog on the ground' - dogs walk on soil, and this lichen grows on soil, unlike tree-dwelling relatives.
contextualKnowledge: The dog pelt lichen is currently under scientific scrutiny as researchers suspect what we call 'Peltigera canina' may actually be several closely related species masquerading under one name. This means future field guides might split this familiar lichen into multiple species as DNA studies reveal hidden diversity.
compareHints: Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside. While freckled pelt lichen also grows on soil, it has distinctive white spots (cephalodia) on its upper surface that dog pelt lacks. The fan pelt lichen has similar veining but typically grows on rocks or tree bases rather than forest soil.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
